By default, NATS waits up to 10 seconds for the `nats-server` to send the initial "ready" signal, [1]. If the server is not ready after this time, the service will signal a failure to start. [NATS clients shuffle the server list on reconnect to prevent a _thundering herd_ situation where all clients try to reconnect to the same server immediately, thus creating a denial of service attack.](4) This shuffling is not necessary if only one server is used, as there is no need to connect to a different server. The setting has no effect when there is only a single server available.](4)

To confirm that the server has received published messages, a client uses [PING/PONG interaction] (connecting/pingpong.md) built into the NATS protocol. When an application calls `flush`, most libraries will put a PING on the outgoing queue of messages and wait for the server to respond with a PONG before saying that the flush was successful [1]. 

Concerning whether pings sent this way count towards the outstanding ping limit, it is stated that even though the client may use PING/PONG for flush, pings sent this way do not count towards [max outgoing pings] (connecting/pingpong.md) [1].

By default, a JetStream key-value bucket keeps a history depth of 1 [3]. To raise that to more than 64, your use case will be better implemented using the Stream functionality directly rather than the KV abstraction, as the maximum history size is 64 [3].

Setting it to a higher value would then determine the number of new TLS client connections a single server can accept before rejecting excess connections, capped at that value in any one second window. Therefore, out of the box with the default of 0, a single NATS server will accept no new client connections based on the `connection_rate_limit` setting.

The NATS server gets a default startup delay of up to 10 seconds [1]. To extend this delay, the `NATS_STARTUP_DELAY` environment variable can be set to a suitable duration [1]. For example, to extend it to 30 seconds, you can use `NATS_STARTUP_DELAY=30s`. This will make the NATS server wait up to 30 seconds, but will report the service as RUNNING as soon as the server is ready to accept connections [1].

The default delay between reconnect attempts is [3] * `ReconnectWait time.Duration` Default is `2 * time.Second`. The default number of times a client will retry before giving up is [1] `connect_retries` Default is `0`, do not retry.

[NATS clients shuffle the server list on reconnect to prevent a _thundering herd_ situation, where all clients try to reconnect to the same server simultaneously, leading to a denial of service attack.](4) This behavior is not relevant if only a single server is configured, as there is no need to shuffle a list that contains only one server. [For cases with multiple servers, shuffling the server list helps distribute the reconnect attempts evenly across all servers, preventing any one server from being overwhelmed.](4)

[If only one server is used, reconnecting will immediately occur to that server, without any shuffling, and the reconnect wait and randomization settings will be ignored.](4)

[2] [3]. A client flush actually confirms the server has received the published messages by sending a PING message to the server and waiting for a PONG response. According to [3], even though the client uses the PING/PONG protocol for flush, pings sent this way do not count towards the [max outgoing pings](connecting/pingpong.md).

[3] The JetStream key/value store has a feature you don't usually find in key/value stores: the ability to keep a history of the values associated with a key (rather than just the current value). The depth of the history is specified when the key/value bucket is created, and the default is a history depth of 1 (i.e. no history). The maximum history size is 64, if you need more your use case will be better implemented using the Stream functionality directly (where you can set the max number of messages per subject to any value you want) rather than the KV abstraction.
